facts: The Wakhan Corridor, a narrow strip in the northeast, was created in the 19th century as a buffer so the Russian and British empires would not share a border.
Afghanistan is landlocked and mountainous, with the Hindu Kush running through its centre.
It is one of the world's largest producers of lapis lazuli, mined in Badakhshan for more than 6,000 years.
Armenia was the first state to adopt Christianity as its official religion, traditionally dated to 301.
Mount Ararat is its national symbol and appears on the coat of arms, though the mountain lies inside Turkey.
The Armenian alphabet was created around 405 and is still used essentially unchanged.
Baku sits about 28 metres below sea level, making it the lowest-lying national capital in the world.
The world's first industrially drilled oil well was sunk near Baku in 1846.
Azerbaijan borders Turkey only through Nakhchivan, an exclave separated from the rest of the country by Armenia.
Bahrain is an archipelago of about 50 natural islands plus dozens more created by land reclamation.
It was the first country in the Persian Gulf to discover oil, in 1932, and the first to begin diversifying away from it.
The King Fahd Causeway has linked it by road to Saudi Arabia since 1986.
Bangladesh sits on the world's largest river delta, formed by the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna.
It is among the most densely populated countries on Earth, with more people than Russia in a fraction of the space.
The Sundarbans, shared with India, is the largest mangrove forest in the world and a stronghold of the Bengal tiger.
Bhutan measures progress by Gross National Happiness alongside economic output.
Its constitution requires at least 60% of the country to remain under forest cover; the actual figure is higher.
Gangkhar Puensum is the highest unclimbed mountain in the world, as climbing above 6,000 metres is prohibited.
Brunei is split into two parts, both surrounded by the Malaysian state of Sarawak.
Oil and gas wealth means citizens pay no income tax and receive free healthcare and education.
Around 70% of the country is still covered by rainforest, one of the highest proportions in Asia.
Angkor was the largest pre-industrial urban centre in the world, sprawling across roughly 1,000 square kilometres.
Cambodia's flag is the only national flag that depicts a building.
Tonlé Sap reverses its direction of flow twice a year as the Mekong rises and falls.
China borders fourteen countries, tied with Russia for the most in the world.
The entire country operates on a single time zone despite spanning five geographic ones.
It has more than 100 cities with populations above one million.
Nicosia is the last divided capital city in Europe, split since 1974 by a UN buffer zone.
Cyprus is the third largest island in the Mediterranean, after Sicily and Sardinia.
Copper takes its name from the island, which supplied the ancient Mediterranean world.
Archaeological evidence puts winemaking in Georgia at around 8,000 years ago, the oldest known anywhere.
The Georgian alphabet is one of only a handful of writing systems in the world with no close relatives.
Georgia lies on the boundary between Europe and Asia, and is claimed by both depending on the definition used.
India is the most populous country in the world, having passed China in 2023.
It has 22 languages with official status at national level and hundreds more in daily use.
The whole country runs on a single time zone offset by 30 minutes from GMT.
Indonesia is made up of over 17,000 islands, around 6,000 of which are inhabited.
It sits on the Ring of Fire and has more active volcanoes than any other country.
The government is moving the capital from Jakarta, which is sinking, to a new city called Nusantara in Borneo.
Damavand is the highest volcano in Asia and the highest peak in the Middle East.
Iran's qanats, underground channels that carry water across desert, have been in use for nearly 3,000 years.
Persian is an Indo-European language, unlike Arabic, which belongs to the Semitic family.
The land between the Tigris and Euphrates is Mesopotamia, where the earliest known cities and writing systems appeared.
Iraq holds some of the largest proven oil reserves in the world.
The Mesopotamian Marshes, drained in the 1990s, have been partially re-flooded and are now a World Heritage Site.
The Dead Sea shore, on Israel's eastern edge, is the lowest land elevation on Earth at around 430 metres below sea level.
Hebrew was revived as an everyday spoken language in the 19th and 20th centuries after centuries of liturgical use.
The country spans a sharp climate gradient, from Mediterranean in the north to desert across most of the Negev in the south.
Japan is an archipelago of roughly 14,000 islands, though four of them hold almost the entire population.
About three quarters of the country is mountainous, concentrating cities onto a small share of the land.
Greater Tokyo is the most populous metropolitan area in the world, with around 37 million people.
Petra, carved into sandstone cliffs by the Nabataeans, was lost to the wider world for centuries before being described by a Swiss traveller in 1812.
Jordan is one of the most water-scarce countries on Earth.
Its only significant coastline is a short stretch on the Gulf of Aqaba at the Red Sea.
Kazakhstan is the largest landlocked country in the world, bigger than all of Western Europe combined.
The Baikonur Cosmodrome, leased to Russia, has launched crewed spaceflights since Yuri Gagarin in 1961.
The Aral Sea, once the fourth largest lake on Earth, has largely dried up through Soviet-era irrigation.
Kuwait has almost no natural fresh water and relies on desalination for most of its supply.
Its currency, the dinar, is consistently the highest-valued in the world against the US dollar.
Around 90% of the population lives in and around Kuwait City on the coast.
More than 90% of Kyrgyzstan is mountainous, most of it above 1,500 metres.
Issyk-Kul is the second largest saline lake in the world and never freezes despite the altitude.
Traditional yurt-based herding is still practised in the high summer pastures known as jailoo.
Laos is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia, which is why the Mekong matters so much to its trade and power supply.
It is the most heavily bombed country per capita in history, with unexploded ordnance from the 1960s and 70s still being cleared.
The Mekong forms much of its border and provides most of its electricity through hydropower.
The cedar of Lebanon on the national flag has been prized as timber since antiquity and is mentioned throughout ancient records.
Byblos is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.
Lebanon's political system allocates the presidency, premiership and speakership to different religious communities.
Malaysia is split in two by the South China Sea, with the peninsula on one side and Borneo states on the other.
Putrajaya is the administrative capital, while Kuala Lumpur remains the official one.
Its rainforests are among the oldest in the world, estimated at over 130 million years.
The Maldives is the lowest-lying country in the world, averaging about 1.5 metres above sea level.
It consists of roughly 1,200 coral islands grouped into 26 atolls, with fewer than 200 inhabited.
In 2009 the cabinet held a meeting underwater to draw attention to rising sea levels.
Mongolia is the most sparsely populated sovereign country in the world.
Ulaanbaatar is the coldest national capital on Earth by average annual temperature.
A significant share of the population still lives nomadically or semi-nomadically in gers.
The capital moved from Yangon to the purpose-built city of Naypyidaw in 2005.
Bagan holds over 2,000 surviving temples and pagodas built between the 11th and 13th centuries.
Myanmar produces most of the world's high-quality rubies, chiefly from the Mogok valley.
Eight of the world's fourteen peaks above 8,000 metres lie wholly or partly in Nepal.
Its flag is the only national flag that is not a rectangle or square.
Nepal was never colonised, and its clocks run 45 minutes off GMT, an offset used by no other country.
The Korean Demilitarized Zone separating it from South Korea is among the most heavily fortified borders in the world.
Paektu Mountain, an active volcano on the Chinese border, holds a central place in national mythology.
The country uses its own Juche calendar, counting years from the birth of Kim Il-sung in 1912.
Oman controls the southern side of the Strait of Hormuz, through which much of the world's seaborne oil passes.
The Musandam Peninsula is an Omani exclave separated from the rest of the country by the United Arab Emirates.
Its aflaj irrigation channels, some over 1,500 years old, still distribute water by gravity across the interior.
K2 is the second highest mountain on Earth and considered far more dangerous to climb than Everest.
The Indus Valley Civilisation, centred on sites such as Mohenjo-daro, was contemporary with ancient Egypt.
Pakistan has the largest glacial ice mass outside the polar regions, in the Karakoram.
Palestine is a UN non-member observer state, recognised by a large majority of member countries.
Its territory is in two separated parts, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.
Jericho in the West Bank is among the oldest continuously inhabited settlements known.
The Philippines comprises about 7,600 islands, of which roughly 2,000 are inhabited.
It lies on the Ring of Fire and in the main typhoon belt, making it one of the most disaster-exposed countries.
The Philippine Trench off its east coast plunges to over 10,000 metres.
Qatar has the world's third largest natural gas reserves despite its small size.
It is a peninsula with a single land border, and almost the entire population lives in or near Doha.
It hosted the 2022 FIFA World Cup, the first held in the Arab world.
Saudi Arabia has no permanent rivers, the largest country in the world without one.
The Rub' al Khali, or Empty Quarter, is the largest continuous sand desert on Earth.
Mecca and Medina, the two holiest cities in Islam, draw millions of pilgrims each year.
Singapore is one of only three surviving sovereign city-states, alongside Monaco and Vatican City.
It has grown around 25% in land area since independence through reclamation.
It has four official languages: English, Malay, Mandarin and Tamil.
Around half of South Korea's population lives in the Seoul metropolitan area.
It went from one of the world's poorest countries in the 1950s to a leading industrial economy within four decades.
Hangul, its alphabet, was purpose-designed in the 15th century rather than evolving gradually.
Sri Lanka's administrative capital is Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, though Colombo remains the commercial centre.
It is one of the world's largest tea exporters, a trade established under British rule in the 19th century.
Sigiriya, a palace complex built atop a 180-metre rock column, dates from the 5th century.
Damascus is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.
Aleppo's ancient souks were one of the largest covered market complexes anywhere before the recent conflict.
The Euphrates crosses the country from Turkey to Iraq and supplies most of its fresh water.
Over 90% of Tajikistan is mountainous, and roughly half of it lies above 3,000 metres.
The Fedchenko Glacier is among the longest glaciers outside the polar regions.
Tajik is a variety of Persian, setting it apart from the Turkic languages of its Central Asian neighbours.
Thailand is the only Southeast Asian country never colonised by a European power.
Bangkok's full ceremonial name is among the longest place names in the world.
It is one of the largest rice exporters globally and a major producer of natural rubber.
Timor-Leste became fully independent in 2002, making it one of the youngest sovereign states.
It occupies the eastern half of Timor island plus the Oecusse exclave inside Indonesian territory.
Portuguese and Tetum are the official languages, a legacy of four centuries of Portuguese rule.
Istanbul is the only major city in the world spanning two continents, split by the Bosphorus.
Göbekli Tepe in the southeast contains monumental structures older than Stonehenge by roughly 6,000 years.
Turkey controls the Bosphorus and Dardanelles, the sole sea route between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean.
The Karakum Desert covers around 70% of Turkmenistan, leaving most of the population along its southern fringe and river oases.
The Darvaza gas crater, alight since the 1970s, is known as the Door to Hell.
Ashgabat holds a record for the highest concentration of white marble buildings of any city.
The United Arab Emirates is a federation of seven emirates, formed in 1971.
Abu Dhabi is the capital and holds most of the oil, while Dubai built its economy on trade and services.
Well over 80% of residents are foreign nationals, one of the highest proportions anywhere.
Uzbekistan is one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world, along with Liechtenstein.
Samarkand and Bukhara were among the great trading cities of the Silk Road.
It is one of the world's leading cotton producers, a legacy of Soviet irrigation that helped drain the Aral Sea.
Vietnam is the world's second largest coffee exporter, specialising in robusta.
Hạ Long Bay contains roughly 1,600 limestone islands and islets, most of them uninhabited.
The country stretches over 1,600 kilometres north to south but narrows to under 50 kilometres at its waist.
Socotra island hosts hundreds of plant species found nowhere else, including the dragon's blood tree.
Sanaa's old city has been inhabited for more than 2,500 years and is built in distinctive tower houses.
Coffee takes its trade name Mocha from the Yemeni port that first exported it widely.
